summary: Quan Vuong opens by stating PI's mission: a single model controlling any robot for any task, acknowledging multiple scientific breakthroughs are still needed. He contrasts old robotics (constrained factory environments, repetitive motions) with modern semi-structured manipulation, attributing progress to VLA models. Tobias Springberg explains VLAs as adaptations of VLMs: they take text, images, and robot joint states as input and produce continuous actions rather than text. He identifies three key engineering challenges: (1) data sourcing for robotics (a trillion-dollar question), (2) adapting model architectures for high-frequency robot control, and (3) the lack of standard deployment infrastructure. PI built its data engine from scratch using teleoperation via leader arms, collecting over 10,000 hours of successful episodes in six months across hundreds of tasks, starting from the 3,800-hour Open X-Embodiment dataset. Tobias traces VLA evolution from RT2 (2023) through dextrous multi-robot models like PI0 (late 2024) to PIO5, which combines a pretrained transformer backbone with a dedicated action expert transformer running at higher frequency via diffusion flow matching. PIO5 can subdivide high-level language requests into subtasks and perform long-horizon tasks up to 10 minutes per episode in entirely unseen homes—the first true sign of broad generalization from VLA training. A generalization study showed that increasing the number of training homes improves held-out scene performance, even surpassing training with the held-out scene specifically. Quan then demonstrates cross-hardware deployment: a robot PI never touched, running far from their office, making coffee end-to-end, illustrating that software and model intelligence—not hardware—is the main bottleneck to scaling. PI is openly partnering with companies (even sharing model checkpoints directly) and aggressively hiring across all roles.
whyItMatters: The talk connects its engineering abstractions, implementation choices, and AI/product implications into one practical system view.

takeaways: PI's mission is a single model that controls any robot to perform any task, requiring multiple scientific breakthroughs across science, engineering, and operations.
VLA models adapt VLMs by adding robot state inputs and producing continuous action outputs via diffusion, enabling direct high-frequency robot control.
The core open challenge for VLA training is data sourcing—described as a trillion-dollar question for the robotics industry.
PI built its data pipeline from scratch using teleoperation via leader arms, collecting over 10,000 hours of successful episodes in six months.

PIO5 combines a pretrained transformer with a dedicated action expert that runs at higher frequency and produces continuous actions via diffusion flow matching, enabling long-horizon tasks up to 10 minutes.

PIO5 demonstrates the first true sign of broad generalization from VLA training, performing cleaning tasks in entirely unseen homes and subdividing high-level requests like 'clean my bedroom' into subtasks.
Increasing the number of training homes improves held-out performance, even surpassing training with the held-out scene specifically—evidence that diverse data scales generalize.
PI deployed its model on a robot it never touched, making coffee end-to-end, showing that software and model intelligence—not hardware—is the primary scaling bottleneck.
PI openly partners with companies (sharing model checkpoints directly) and is aggressively hiring across all roles, citing talent as their biggest bottleneck.
Understand what Vision Language Action models are and how they differ from VLMs.

sections.title: Introduction and Mission
sections.summary: Quan Vuong introduces PI's mission to build a model controlling any robot for any task, noting scientific breakthroughs are still needed. He contrasts traditional constrained robotics with modern semi-structured manipulation capabilities.

sections.title: What Are Vision Language Action Models?
sections.summary: Tobias explains VLAs as adaptations of VLMs for robotics: they take text, images, and robot state (joint positions) as input and produce actions to control robots directly, rather than text answers.

sections.title: Engineering Challenges for VLA Training
sections.summary: Tobias contrasts VLM and VLA training pipelines, identifying three challenges: open data sources (trillion-dollar question), architecture adaptation for high-frequency control, and lack of deployment infrastructure for on-premise robot policies.

sections.title: PI's Data Engine
sections.summary: Details PI's from-scratch data pipeline: human operators teleoperate robots via leader arms, collecting data around the clock across expanding task sets. Data is annotated in the cloud and used for model training. PI0 model shown performing autonomous shirt folding.

sections.title: Data Scale and Growth
sections.summary: Starting from the 3,800-hour Open X-Embodiment dataset, PI collected 10,000 hours of successful episodes in six months across tens of environments and hundreds of tasks. After another six months, data expanded further with mobile manipulation setups across hundreds of scenes.

sections.title: VLA Industry Evolution and PIO5
sections.summary: Tobias traces VLA evolution as time-lagged relative to VLMs: RT2 (2023), dextrous multi-robot VLAs including PI0 (mid-late 2024), and now PIO5 with open-world generalization. PIO5 trains on static, mobile, and web multimodal data using a pretrained transformer expanded with an action expert transformer.

sections.title: PIO5 Capabilities: Long-Horizon Tasks and Generalization
sections.summary: Tobias shows PIO5 subdividing high-level requests like 'clean my bedroom' into subtasks (pick up pillow, make bed, throw away trash). The action expert transformer attends to VLM internals and produces continuous actions via diffusion flow matching. PIO5 performs long-horizon tasks up to 10 minutes in entirely unseen homes—the first true sign of broad generalization from VLA training. A generalization study shows increasing training homes improves held-out performance, even surpassing training with the held-out scene specifically.

sections.title: Partnerships and Cross-Hardware Deployment
sections.summary: Quan demonstrates a robot PI never touched, running far from their office, making coffee end-to-end, arguing software and model intelligence—not hardware—is the main scaling bottleneck. PI openly partners with companies, even sharing model checkpoints directly for inference. Quan identifies talent as PI's biggest bottleneck and announces aggressive hiring across all roles.

demonstrations: Video of a robot folding clothes from a dryer, placing them in a basket, bringing to a table, and folding them.
Video of humanoid robot dancing to show complex physical motion capabilities.

Dashboard showing scheduled data collection sessions with operators performing specific episodes.
Video of PI0 model autonomously performing shirt folding.
Video of a mobile manipulation setup with an autonomously running policy.
Video of PIO5 performing cleaning tasks (surface cleaning, trash disposal, bed making) in an unseen home, prompted by colleague Chelsea.

Video of a robot PI never touched, located far from their office, making a cup of coffee end-to-end.
limitations: PI's ultimate goal of a model controlling any robot for any task is not ready today and requires multiple scientific breakthroughs.
There is no standard solution for deploying large robot policies on-premise or on-device for robots.
Early VLAs like RT2 were held back by lack of available robot data.
The data source for robotics training remains an open question.
Talent acquisition is PI's biggest bottleneck to progress.
The problem of universal robot control is far from being solved across scientific, engineering, and operational dimensions.
quantitativeClaims: Open X-Embodiment was the biggest publicly available dataset at approximately 3,800 hours of data.
After six months of data collection, PI had collected about 10,000 hours of successful episodes across tens of environments and hundreds of tasks.
After another six months, PI collected many more hours including significant mobile manipulation data across hundreds of scenes.
PIO5 can perform long-horizon tasks of up to 10 minutes per episode.
Over 50% of the work in building capable robot policies is getting the data pipeline right.
